html: In 1948 the United Nations General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Article 26 states that everyone has the right to education, that it shall be free at least in the elementary and fundamental stages, and that it "shall be directed to the full development of the human personality and to the strengthening of respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms" [1]. The 2030 Agenda carries the same commitment forward as Sustainable Development Goal 4, "ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all", and Target 4.7 asks that every learner gain the knowledge and skills needed to promote sustainable development [2].

html: Access to information is not the same as education that changes what people do. Science-communication research has long questioned the "deficit model", the assumption that people hold mistaken views because they lack facts. Knowledge does shape attitudes, but the relationship is far more nuanced than the model assumes [3], and the model persists for reasons that include how scientists are trained and how they imagine their audiences [4]. Research on pro-environmental behavior documents the same distance between knowing and doing [5].

Science-communication research has long questioned the "deficit model", the assumption that people hold mistaken views because they lack facts. Knowledge does shape attitudes, but the relationship is far more nuanced than the model assumes [3], and the model persists for reasons that include how scientists are trained and how they imagine their audiences [4]. html: Our own survey pointed the same way. Most respondents already understood that visible mold is a problem, so a lecture saying "mold is dangerous" would have repeated what many people knew. The gap was in the risks that cannot be seen: only 58% understood that a normal look and smell does not mean no risk, and even respondents with higher knowledge often did not act on it. We went looking for what the research suggests works instead: active learning raised exam performance by 0.47 standard deviations and lowered failure rates (21.8% against 33.8%) across 225 science, engineering, and mathematics studies [6], and in a meta-analysis of serious-games studies, serious games outperformed conventional instruction on learning (d = 0.29) and retention (d = 0.36), though they were not more motivating [7]. These studies come from formal courses, so we treat them as direction, not proof, and we test our own tools on our own audiences.

html: Synthetic biology adds a second reason to engage. The Royal Academy of Engineering's early public dialogue on the field called for an active and ongoing public engagement programme, with platforms for people to share their views on both the benefits and the concerns [8]. AeroSense puts a fly olfactory receptor into a cultured human cell line and reads it with a fly-inspired circuit. We wanted people to understand that, and to tell us what they thought of it.

html: We began by assuming that the problem was a lack of knowledge about mold. Our survey tested that assumption and revealed a narrower need. Most respondents knew mold was dangerous, but many still trusted heat, appearance or smell to judge whether food was safe. Every activity on this page carries that one testable claim from first contact, through structured learning, to outside feedback and handover. Learning Lab learners answered the three misconception statements correctly far more often than the survey baseline did, with the largest gap, 28 percentage points, on heating.

html: On September 23, 2026, a member of our model team gave a research-sharing lecture on our electronic-nose work to more than thirty undergraduate and graduate students at China Medical University. The lecture followed one thread: why electronic noses drift and why recalibrating them is costly; how the insect olfactory system keeps its odor code stable; and how our spiking neural network borrows those ideas. We also presented the results that do not flatter the model: the 14 sensors in our test dataset behave like only three types, adding more features did not help once the data had been compressed, and accuracy fell to about 75% when odors were presented continuously. We taught the evidence together with its limits so that listeners could judge the method themselves.

html: Learners told us two things, and we changed the platform in response. First, the interface was unclear and the opening had too much text, so we cut the text and separated sections with color blocks. Second, the opening was too difficult. To make the platform accessible to more people, we lowered the difficulty of the opening and closing sections and added hands-on tasks, so that learners understand by doing.

html: We ran a bilingual (Chinese and English) online questionnaire on mold and mycotoxin understanding, food-storage habits and what people want from a screening tool. It reached 300 respondents. Three findings shaped the rest of our education work:
text: We ran a bilingual (Chinese and English) online questionnaire on mold and mycotoxin understanding, food-storage habits and what people want from a screening tool. It reached 300 respondents. Three findings shaped the rest of our education work:

html: Public understanding varies by risk concept. People were most secure about the risk they can see. 78% understood that removing visible mold does not always make food safe. Understanding was lower for heat, where 64% understood that heating does not always destroy all mycotoxins, and lowest for looks and smell, where only 58% understood that a normal look and smell does not mean no risk. On that last item 27% were unsure and 15% held the misconception. The risks that cannot be seen are the ones people understand least, and they are the risks our sensor is meant to address.（圖片解釋）

Understanding was lower for heat, where 64% understood that heating does not always destroy all mycotoxins, and lowest for looks and smell, where only 58% understood that a normal look and smell does not mean no risk. On that last item 27% were unsure and 15% held the misconception. The risks that cannot be seen are the ones people understand least, and they are the risks our sensor is meant to address.（圖片解釋）

html: Knowledge does not automatically translate into practice. We compared respondents with higher knowledge (n = 180) with those with lower or uncertain knowledge (n = 120). Higher-knowledge respondents were more likely to record the opening date (42% against 25%) and to report a recommended storage practice (71% against 46%). But even in the higher-knowledge group, 58% did not record the opening date. Knowing the facts helped, but it did not close the gap between knowing and doing.（圖片解釋）

html: Users value trustworthy, actionable results. Asked what they need from a screening tool, respondents chose trustworthiness of results (76%) and accuracy, including avoiding false negatives (73%) first, followed by clear next-step guidance (68%). These ranked ahead of ease of use (61%), affordable cost per test (54%) and a fast result (49%). People do not only want a number; they want to trust it and know what to do next.（圖片解釋）

html: The survey changed what we built. Because understanding was weakest for invisible risks, we made the claim that heat and looks and smell cannot tell you whether food is safe the center of the game and of Module 2 of the Learning Lab, which use the same statements as the survey so that later results can be compared with this baseline. Because knowledge did not automatically become practice, we added habits, such as recording the opening date, to the curriculum and our posts alongside the facts. Because people want trust and a clear next step, the Learning Lab teaches what a screening result does and does not certify, and what to do after each result, and our design prioritizes avoiding missed risk.

html: Why does it matter?
text: Why does it matter?

html: Our survey showed that the gaps are not missing facts but untested trust: many people were unsure whether heat or a sniff test can tell them food is safe. Being told "a sniff test is not a safety test" twice does not change that trust. Learners need to experience why smell can mislead.
text: Our survey showed that the gaps are not missing facts but untested trust: many people were unsure whether heat or a sniff test can tell them food is safe. Being told "a sniff test is not a safety test" twice does not change that trust. Learners need to experience why smell can mislead.

html: Smell works by pattern, not by a single signal. An odor activates several receptors at once, similar odors produce similar patterns, and mixtures overlap. This is why a nose, human or electronic, can be fooled, and it is also the principle AeroSense is built on. Odor Pixel Suite lets learners make the decisions themselves: recognize a pattern, follow a scent, separate a mixture, and see when they get it wrong. The games turn the reason behind our survey findings and the logic of our sensor into something learners can play.

Draft design
We started from three perspectives on scent: its encoding features, its identity and identification, and its composition ratio. We sketched one game for each: pattern recognition, a scent-guided labyrinth and a fingerprint mixer.

html:
Internal playtest & refinement
Our teammates played the first versions. One could not pass even the easiest level. Another said the instructions gave no idea where to start. A third said the games matched our design intent, but that our target audience might need to be redefined. We learned that what felt easy to the designers was not easy for anyone else.

html:
Public playtest & feedback
We tested the prototypes with 32 people. In Pattern Recognition, players said there were too many patterns to remember. In the Mixer, players reported that they never succeeded and found it too complex. In the Labyrinth, players said the controls were not smooth and did not understand what the E and Q keys did.

html:
Camp/workshop deployment
At the Shan-chi Elementary School science camp, we projected the game for the whole class. The pupils found it too difficult at first, so we adjusted the difficulty and created three levels, letting each group find a suitable option. One pupil wrote on a worksheet: "Today I played the memory game. It was really hard! I thought it was really fun!”

html:
Data + optional external release
The released version answers what we heard. Junior levels use smaller patterns and let players review before the quiz. The Junior Mixer starts with two scent cards and a simple mix. Challenge levels use closer lookalikes and hidden patterns for players who want more. For educators, workshops can switch on paired pre/post questions with anonymous data export, while everyday visitors are never quizzed. Progress is stored only in the player's own browser.

html: The games taught us three things.
text: The games taught us three things.

html: First, difficulty is a design decision, not a detail. Teammates, members of the public and primary-school pupils all hit the same wall at the start. Three levels now let each learner begin where they can succeed, and the same structure lets a teacher use one game from primary school to university.

html: Second, fun is not the same as learning. At the camp, many worksheets mentioned only that the game was fun. This is why each game now links to a Science page and why educators can add paired pre/post questions. These let us measure learning, not just enjoyment, in future workshops.

html: Third, players' struggles confirmed our own design. When players could not remember enough patterns, or could not separate overlapping fingerprints by eye, they experienced the exact problem AeroSense is built to solve. Humans are poor at decoding overlapping receptor patterns, which is why our sensor relies on computational decoding rather than on a person reading the signal.

html:
Post 1, Parts Design: "We put a fruit fly's nose inside a human cell."
Explains how a fruit fly odor receptor and a calcium-sensitive glow protein, placed in human cells, turn a smell into light: an odor molecule binds the receptor, calcium flows in, and the cell lights up. The brighter the glow, the stronger the smell.
